dataset.name: Soil properties and root characteristics across four lowland Panamanian forests from 0 - 1 m soil depths
description: Fine roots significantly influence ecosystem-scale cycling of nutrients, carbon (C), and water, yet there is limited understanding of how fine root traits vary across and within tropical forests, some of Earth's most C-rich ecosystems. The biomass of fine roots can impact soil carbon storage, as root mortality is a primary source of new carbon to soils. A positive relationship has been observed between fine root biomass and soil carbon stocks in Panama (Cusack et al 2018). Beyond biomass, root characteristics like specific root length (SRL) could also influence soil carbon, as roots with higher SRL are less dense and thinner, potentially decomposing more easily or promoting soil aggregation. Understanding the effects of root morphology and tissue quality on soil carbon storage and with soil properties in general can improve predictions of landscape-scale carbon patterns. We aggregated new data of root biomass, morphology and nutrient content at 0-10 cm, 10-20 cm, 20-50 cm and 50-100 cm depth increments across four distinct lowland Panamanian forests and paired with already published datasets (Cusack et al 2018; Cusack and Turner 2020) of soil chemistry from the same sites and soil depths to explore relationship between soil carbon stocks and root characteristics.

The datasets provided include .csv and .xlsx files for fine root characteristics and soil chemistry from four different forests across 0-10 cm, 10-20 cm, 20-50 cm, and 50-100 cm depth increments. Root characteristics include live fine root biomass, dead fine root biomass, coarse root biomass, specific root length, root diameter, root tissue density, specific root area, root %N, root %C, and root C/N ratio. Soil chemistry data includes total carbon (TC), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), bulk density, total phosphorus (TP), available phosphorus (AEM Pi), and various Mehlich-extractable elements such as aluminum, calcium, iron, potassium, manganese, phosphorus, and zinc. Nitrogen content measures include ammonium, nitrate, total dissolved nitrogen (TDN), dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN), and dissolved organic nitrogen (DON). The dataset also includes total exchangeable bases (TEB) and effective cation exchange capacity (ECEC) in both centimoles of charge per kilogram and micromoles of charge per gram. The soil chemistry data was obtained from Cusack et al (2018) and Cusack and Turner (2020) and paired with root characteristics data for the same depth increments and sites. Additionally, a .kml file is provided with coordinates for all 32 plots included in the study across four forests (n = 8 plots per site). Root data was averaged across these 8 plots per site and soil data was collected in one pit in each site. This dataset serves as baseline data before a throughfall exclusion experiment, Panama Rainforest Changes with Experimental Drying (PARCHED), was implemented. No special software is needed to open these files.

measurementTechnique: This study was conducted in four distinct lowland seasonal tropical forests located across gradients in rainfall and soil fertility on the Isthmus of Panama. The sites are a subset of a larger network of ~50 1-ha long-term plots maintained by the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) in the Panamanian lowlands. The four forests span an increase of 1,000 mm MAP, and include three forests on strongly weathered, low fertility soils at low (site GIG), mid (site P12), and high rainfall (site SC), and one forest on high-fertility soils paired with the infertile forest at mid-rainfall (site P13). This design was used to help disentangle effects of mean annual precipitation (MAP) and soil fertility on soil responses to seasonal and experimental drying. The four forests included here were: a forest at 2350 mm MAP on strongly weathered, infertile soil on the Gigante Peninsula (GIG), two paired forests at 2600 mm MAP on the Buena Vista Peninsula, one with strongly weathered infertile soil (Plot 12 [P12]), and one with less weathered fertile soil (Plot 13 [P13]), and a forest at 3421 mm MAP on strongly weathered infertile soil on the Caribbean coast in the San Lorenzo forest at Sherman Crane (SC).

Soil chemistry: Soil chemistry was assessed using methods from Cusack et al. (2018) and Cusack and Turner (2020). Soil cores were collected from five locations within each 1-hectare plot at depths of 0–10 cm, 10–20 cm, 20–50 cm, and 50–100 cm. The top 20 cm was sampled with a 5 cm diameter corer, while deeper samples were taken with a 6.25 cm diameter auger. An additional eight surface samples (0–10 cm) were collected per plot, totaling 13 surface samples. Samples were air-dried, sieved, ground and then analyzed for soil chemistry.

Root Collection: Root biomass was sampled to a depth of 1.2 meters using a 5-cm diameter hand auger. This sampling was performed in conjunction with the installation of minirhizotron tubes at a 45° angle to the soil surface (Norby et al., 2004). Due to the angled sampling, cores were collected in 14.1 cm length increments to ensure true vertical depths were in 10-cm intervals. One hole in each 10 x 10 meter plot was sampled, with plots spaced more than 10 meters apart within each forest (n = 8 per site). Samples were stored in plastic bags at 4°C and processed within a year of collection. Soil collection occurred in September 2017 (P12), December 2017 (P13), February 2018 (SC), and October 2018 (GIG), corresponding to the late wet season for P12, P13, and GIG, and the transition to the dry season in SC (Paton, 2023a, b). In total, 384 samples were collected across sites and depths.

Root Processing: Wet weights of all field samples were measured. Subsamples of 3 – 4 grams of root-free, fresh soil were oven-dried at 105°C until a constant weight was reached to determine soil moisture content and dry weight for each depth increment. Fresh soil was rinsed through a 0.25 mm sieve to remove soil from roots, which were then cleaned manually using paint brushes and water. Roots were sorted into fine (< 2 mm in diameter) and coarse (> 2 mm in diameter) categories using a caliper. Coarse roots in the collected cores were generally no larger than 3 mm, thus representing a relatively small-diameter portion of the coarse root stock. Fine roots were further classified as live or dead through visual and mechanical assessments, with live roots identified by their turgidity and intact cortex and periderm (Freschet et al., 2021a). Live fine roots were scanned to assess morphology, then dried at 60°C until a constant weight was achieved to measure biomass. Root biomass per soil mass was calculated using dry root and dry soil mass per sample (g-biomass / kg dry soil). Cumulative root biomass to 1.2 meters depth was calculated in mg/cm² by dividing the total fine root biomass for the soil profile by the soil core surface area. Standing root biomass carbon stocks were also calculated (mg C/cm²).

Root Morphology and Chemistry: Live fine root samples were scanned at 800 dpi using a 9800XL plus-Microtek-TMA 1600 II scanner. The images were analyzed with WinRHIZO software to determine specific root length (SRL), specific root area (SRA), root tissue density (RTD), and mean root diameter. SRL (cm * mg⁻¹) represents root length per dry mass; SRA (cm² * mg⁻¹) represents root surface area per dry mass; and RTD (g * cm⁻³) represents root dry mass per volume. After drying, live root tissues were finely ground for elemental C and N analysis using a Carlo-Erba NA1500 at the Environmental Stable Isotope Laboratory at Duke University. Root chemistry was analyzed at various depths from 4 – 5 plots per site, depending on tissue availability. To calculate standing fine root carbon stocks, we multiplied the mg-biomass by the site-average fine root %C.
